subject: english-language
topicDisplay: Component 1: 20th-Century Literature Reading and Creative Prose Writing
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A simile compares two things using:
questions.explain: A simile is an explicit comparison using 'like' or 'as'.

questions.q: A metaphor is a technique that:
options: Describes something as if it is something else
Repeats the first letter of words
questions.explain: A metaphor states one thing is another to create meaning.

options: Drawing conclusions from implicit evidence in the text
Copying the text word for word
questions.explain: Inference involves reading between the lines to work out implied meaning.

questions.q: To analyse a writer's methods you should comment on:
options: Language, structure and their effect on the reader
questions.explain: Analysis links technique to its effect on the reader.

options: Gives human qualities to something non-human
questions.explain: Personification attributes human characteristics to objects, animals or ideas.

options: The weather or setting reflects a mood or emotion
questions.explain: Pathetic fallacy uses nature/weather to mirror mood or foreshadow events.

questions.q: A first-person narrative is written using:
questions.explain: First-person narration uses 'I', giving a personal viewpoint.

questions.q: A writer describes a storm growing violent as a character becomes angry. This is an example of:
questions.explain: The setting mirrors the character's emotional state — pathetic fallacy.

questions.q: 'Show, don't tell' in creative writing means:
options: Convey feelings through detail and action rather than stating them
Use as few words as possible
questions.explain: Showing through sensory detail engages the reader more than plain statement.

questions.q: An effective opening to a piece of creative writing should:
questions.explain: A strong opening grabs attention through action, description or intrigue.

questions.q: Varying sentence lengths in creative writing:
options: Creates rhythm and can build tension or emphasis
questions.explain: Short sentences can add impact; longer ones develop detail.

options: Focus on one main idea or topic
questions.explain: Well-structured paragraphs develop one idea, linked with connectives.

questions.q: Sensory description appeals to the reader's:
questions.explain: Sensory detail helps the reader imagine the scene vividly.

questions.q: To create tension in a story, a writer might:
options: Use short sentences and withhold information
questions.explain: Pace and suspense are built by controlling sentence length and information.

questions.q: When commenting on structure, you might discuss:
options: How a text begins, develops and shifts focus
questions.explain: Structural analysis considers openings, shifts, focus and endings.

options: Repetition of the same initial consonant sound
A human quality given to objects
questions.explain: Alliteration repeats initial sounds for effect, e.g. 'sea's slow surge'.

questions.q: Using a range of ambitious vocabulary in creative writing should:
options: Be accurate and suit the context
Always be as long as possible
questions.explain: Vocabulary should be precise and appropriate, not merely complex.

questions.q: A question that asks how a writer 'creates a sense of fear' requires you to:
options: Select methods and explain their effect on the reader
Give your opinion of the author
questions.explain: Such questions reward analysis of technique and effect, supported by quotation.

specSource: Eduqas GCSE English Language specification; Component 1
